sections.h: 1 Esdras 1–2: from Josiah to the halt
sections.b: The book's first two chapters retell 2 Chronicles 35:1–36:21, Ezra 1 and Ezra 4:7–24 in Greek. Chapter 1 keeps the order of Chronicles, adds two verses on Josiah's upright heart and the judgment already decreed (1 Esdras 1:21–22), and changes many details: Jeremiah, not Pharaoh, gives the warning Josiah ignores (1 Esdras 1:26), and the names of Josiah's sons are shuffled (1 Esdras 1:32; 1 Esdras 1:41). Chapter 2 joins Cyrus's decree and the return of the vessels to the Artaxerxes letter, which it places before Darius and makes about the temple as well as the walls (1 Esdras 2:15–25). That order sets up the story of the three guards in chapters 3–4. On this site 1 Esdras is numbered as in Swete's Greek; the letter of 1 Esdras 2:15–25 is 2:16–30 in the KJV.

common: 1 Esdras 1–2 is a Greek retelling of the end of Chronicles and parts of Ezra, with few facts not found in those books.
uncommon: Some hold that 1 Esdras keeps an older arrangement of the Ezra material, not a rearrangement of the Ezra we have.

sections.b: 1 Esdras opens with Josiah's Passover (1 Esdras 1:1–20) and adds what Chronicles lacks: his "works stood upright before his Lord, for they came from a heart full of godliness," yet the words of the Lord had already risen up against Israel (1 Esdras 1:21–22). At Megiddo he dies because he "did not listen to the words of Jeremiah the prophet from the mouth of the Lord" (1 Esdras 1:26), where Chronicles has Neco's words "from God's mouth." The Talmud reaches a similar verdict (Taanit 22b); Josephus blames fate (Antiquities 10.76).

1 Esdras retells Josiah's Passover from 2 Chronicles 35 with Greek touches: the priests are robed, the Levites hold the unleavened bread, the Passover is "roasted" (as Exodus 12:9 requires), and the feast is the greatest "since the days of Samuel the prophet" (1 Esdras 1:2–18). Where the Hebrew says "And so with the cattle," both Greek books read the same letters as "morning" (1 Esdras 1:10). The book later sets the returned exiles' Passover beside this one (1 Esdras 7:10–15).

1 Esdras gives Jeremiah a larger part than Chronicles does. The warning Josiah ignored at Megiddo comes "from the mouth of the Lord" through Jeremiah (1 Esdras 1:26); Jeremiah laments Josiah (1 Esdras 1:30); Zedekiah "paid no respect to the words spoken by Jeremiah the prophet" (1 Esdras 1:45); and the seventy years end with Cyrus "to fulfill the LORD's word from Jeremiah's mouth" (1 Esdras 2:1).

1 Esdras 1:47–55 follows 2 Chronicles 36:14–21 closely, with a few Greek changes: God is "the King of their ancestors" in Vaticanus (1 Esdras 1:48), the Chaldeans come with "kings" (1 Esdras 1:49), and "the LORD's chests" go to Babylon with the holy vessels (1 Esdras 1:51), where Alexandrinus has the vessels of the ark instead.

1 Esdras keeps Chronicles' reading of Jeremiah's seventy years as the land's Sabbath rest, in the future tense: "All the time it lies desolate it will keep Sabbath, until seventy years are filled up" (1 Esdras 1:55), and goes straight on to Cyrus "to fulfill the LORD's word from Jeremiah's mouth" (1 Esdras 2:1).

In 1 Esdras Cyrus says that "The Lord of Israel, the Lord Most High, has appointed me king of the whole inhabited world" (1 Esdras 2:3), where Ezra has "All the kingdoms of the earth the LORD, the God of the heavens, has given me" (Ezra 1:2). Josephus follows the Greek ("king of the habitable earth") and adds that Cyrus had read Isaiah's prophecy of him (Antiquities 11.3–5).

1 Esdras calls Sheshbazzar "Sanassar, the leader of Judea" (1 Esdras 2:11) and, two verses later, "Samanassar" (1 Esdras 2:14), in Codex Vaticanus; Alexandrinus, the KJV and Josephus have Sanabassar. Its list of the vessels he brought adds up to its total of 5,469 (1 Esdras 2:12–13), unlike Ezra's (Ezra 1:9–11).

sections.h: Why the work stopped, in 1 Esdras
sections.b: 1 Esdras makes the Artaxerxes letter of Ezra 4 the cause of the long halt in the temple work. The officials complain of a temple as well as walls (1 Esdras 2:17–18), and when the king agrees, "Work on the temple in Jerusalem stopped, and it stayed stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of the Persians" (1 Esdras 2:25). In Ezra the letter is about the city and belongs to a later reign.

The letter against Jerusalem in 1 Esdras comes from officials "who lived in Samaria and the other places" (1 Esdras 2:15): Belemus, Mithridates, Tabellius, Rathymus, Beeltethmus and Samellius, Greek forms of the names in Ezra 4:7–9, with the Aramaic title "chief official" read as the name Beeltethmus. These are Persian provincial officials, not the later Samaritan community.

sections.h: 1 Esdras as a witness to Chronicles
sections.b: 1 Esdras 1 is a second Greek translation of 2 Chronicles 35–36, so where it and the Greek of Chronicles agree against the Hebrew they show how the Hebrew was being read. Both have "morning" where the Hebrew has "cattle" (1 Esdras 1:10; 2 Chronicles 35:12) and leading men where the Hebrew has singers (1 Esdras 1:30; 2 Chronicles 35:25). Where they disagree, the two Greek books show that more than one Greek form of these chapters was in use.

1 Esdras, like Chronicles, last mentions the ark when Josiah has it placed in the temple (1 Esdras 1:3–4). At the fall, Vaticanus speaks of "the LORD's chests" (Greek kibōtoi, the word for the ark) carried to Babylon; (1 Esdras 1:51), where Alexandrinus has the vessels of the ark instead.
Where 2 Chronicles 35:15 names Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, 1 Esdras has "Asaph, Zechariah and Eddinus, the king's men" (1 Esdras 1:14). It calls the singers hieropsaltai, "temple harpists."

1 Esdras gives Jehoiachin his father's name, Jehoiakim (Greek Iōakeim), and in Vaticanus uses "Jeconiah" for his uncle Jehoahaz (1 Esdras 1:32; 1 Esdras 1:41). Vaticanus makes him eight years old, as in 2 Chronicles 36:9; Alexandrinus eighteen, as in 2 Kings 24:8.
